requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in rowing activities, including weather- and water-related hazards, and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for the following injuries or illnesses that can occur while rowing: blisters, hypothermia, heat-related illnesses, dehydration, sunburn, sprains, and strains. (c) Review the Scouting America Safety Afloat policy. Explain to your counselor how this applies to rowing activities.

pamphlet_excerpts: Rowing Blisters Likely: In rowing, blisters are most likely to occur on the hands.
Pay Attention Tender: Pay attention to any tender or sensitive areas (hot spots) thatindicate the start of a blister.
Adjust Relaxyour Grip: You may be able to adjust or relaxyour grip to avoid friction on the sensitive area.
Prevent Them Wearing: If you are prone to blisters, prevent them by wearing rowing gloves.
step_by_step_procedure: Cover Protect Area: If you do get a blister, cover and protect the area from further irritation.
Sprain Occurs Ankle: A sprain occurs when an ankle, wrist, or other joint is bent farenough to overstretch the ligaments, the tough bands that holdjoints together.
Strain Occurs Muscles: A strain occurs when muscles are overstretched, creating tears in the muscle fibers.
Minor Sprains Strainscause: Minor sprains and strainscause only mild discomfort, but more serious sprains and strainsmight be temporarily disabling.

pamphlet_excerpts: Whenever Yougo Swimming: Whenever yougo swimming, make sure youhave a buddywith you.
Ifyou Afloat Same: Ifyou go afloat, the same ruleapplies, makesure you have abuddy either withyou or nearby inanother boat.
Rowers Passed America: All rowers must have passed the Scouting America swimmertest.
America Swimmer Test: The Scouting America swimmer test demonstrates the minimum level of swimming ability required for safe deep-waterswimming, a necessary part of safe.
step_by_step_procedure: Pass Followingswimmer Test: To qualify as a “swimmer,” you must pass the followingswimmer test.
Jump Feetfirst Water: Jump feetfirst into water over your headin depth.
Level Off Swim: Level off and swim 75 yards in a strong mannerusing one or more of the following strokes: sidestroke, breaststroke, trudgen, or crawl.
Then Swim Yardsusing: Then swim 25 yardsusing an easy resting backstroke.

pamphlet_excerpts: Aquatics Supervision: Paddle Craft Safety to assist in the planning and conduct of all rowing activities.
Complete Health History: A complete health history is requiredof all participants as evidence of fitness for rowing activities.
Forms Minors Signed: Forms for minors must be signed by a parent or legal guardian.
Participants Asked Relate: Participants should be asked to relate any recent incidents ofillness or injury just prior to the activity.
step_by_step_procedure: Supervision Andprotection: Supervision andprotection should be adjusted to anticipate any potential risksassociated with individual health conditions.
Significanthealth Conditions: For significanthealth conditions, the adult supervisor should require anexamination by a physician and consult with parent, guardian.
Operation Rowing Craft: Operation of rowing craft is generally limited to youth and adults who have completed the Scouting America swimmer classification test.
However Anyone Not: However, anyone not classified as a swimmer may operate a fixed-seat rowboat if accompanied by a buddy who is a swimmer.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Alone or with a passenger, do the following in either a fixed-seat or sliding-seat rowboat: (1) Launch. (2) Row in a straight line for 100 yards. Stop, pivot, and return to the starting point. (3) Backwater in a straight line for 25 yards. Make a turn underway and return to the starting point. (4) Land and moor or rack your craft. (5) Tie the following mooring knots—clove hitch, roundturn with two half-hitches, bowline, Wellman's knot, and mooring hitch. (b) Participate as a rowing team member in a competitive rowing meet. The team may be sponsored by a school, club, or Scout unit. The meet must include competition between two or more teams with different sponsors. Complete at least 10 hours of team practice prior to the meet.

Store Them Upside: Store them upside down onracks where they are protected from sun, wind, andwater.
step_by_step_procedure: Shells Stored Suspended: If shells are stored suspended on racks or inslings, be sure there is adequate support to preventbowing or sagging.

Not Leave Theboat: Do not leave theboat hanging orgrounded at lowtide.

pamphlet_excerpts: Strokes Maneuvers Rowing: The strokes and maneuvers of rowing alone are the same asrowing with a passenger, except that you sit on the midshipseat to maintain trim.
Doing Single-person Launch: When doing a single-person launch from a mooring where thebow is tied out, it is a good idea to ask another boater for help.
Person Assisting Play: The person assisting will play the role of the passenger, exceptthat instead of getting in when you are ready, he or she willgive you a gentle push off.
Available Out Begin: If no one is available to help out, begin by loading yourgear into the boat, then untying the stern painter.
step_by_step_procedure: Sit Thedock Ease: Sit on thedock and ease in over the transom while being careful to notlose your balance.
Move Forward Bow: Move forward to the bow and untie the bowpainter.
Boat Free Pulled: When the boat is free and you have pulled the paintersinto the boat, take your rowing position and move the boataway from the pier.
There Not Enough: If there is not enough space for you to rowout, use one oar over the stern or at the bow to scull or paddleyourself clear of obstacles, then begin.

pamphlet_excerpts: Rescue Procedures His: Rescue Procedures. his or her midship with one hand while maintaining the oars inthe safety position with the other.
Experienced Rowers: Even experienced rowers may occasionally capsize inshells, so you should always have someone in a fixed-seatrowboat or powerboat on the water to assist.
Capsize Canoe Rowing: If you capsize in a canoe rowing rig and the craft swamps, remember to stay with the boat, hang on, do not lose contactwith the canoe.
Slide Gunwaleinto Open: Slide over the gunwaleinto an open area of the craft.
step_by_step_procedure: Sit Flaton Bottom: Sit flaton the bottom and use one oar to paddle to shore where you can empty thecanoe and relaunch.
Overboard Deep Waterand: If you are overboard in deep waterand the canoe rowing rig is still afloat, reenter using the flop-over method.
Begin Placing Oar: Begin by placing the oar blades on abreastplate out of your way.
Then Movealong Gunwale: Then movealong the gunwale to a midship pointwhere there is an open compartment.

pamphlet_excerpts: Friend Boat Capsizes: If you are with a friend and your boat capsizes, pull yourself up over the side of the swamped boat while your friendholds down the other side.
Push Down Gunwale: Push down on the gunwale withboth hands so that you bring yourself up to where your hipsare about level with the gunwale.
Then Roll Sothat: Then roll over sothat you fall into the bottom of the swamped boat, landing onyour backside.
Then Lean Side: You can then lean over the side to counterbalance as your friend follows the same steps to come in over theopposite side.
step_by_step_procedure: Remember Pull Yourself: Remember that when you pull yourself up on the gunwale, the gunwalewill be forced down into the water.
Roll Weightoff Gunwale: After you roll in and get your weightoff the gunwale, it will rise back up.
Fully Awash Gunwaleof: Even when fully awash, the gunwaleof most boats will be a few inches above the level of the water.
Aloneand Boatswamps Yougo: If you are aloneand your boatswamps and yougo over the side, the best way toget back in is overthe transom.

pamphlet_excerpts: Rowboats Variety Materials: Rowboats are made from a variety of materials, includingaluminum, fiberglass, plastic, wood planking, and plywood.
Lightweight Durable Metal: This lightweight, durable metal needs little maintenance.
Aluminum Not Float: Aluminum will not float, but all approved aluminumboats have flotation materials in chambers that keep the boatafloat if it capsizes or swamps.
Easy Cut Drill: Easy to cut and drill, wood is probably theeasiest boatbuilding material to handle.
step_by_step_procedure: Buoyant Boat Wood: It is very buoyant, a boat made from wood planking floats even when it is fullof water.
Cedar Spruce Cypress: Cedar, spruce, cypress, and pine are good plankingwoods.
However Tokeep Craft: However, tokeep such craft watertight, they must be regularly caulkedand painted.
Epoxy Compoundsalso Addedto: Epoxy compoundsalso can be addedto a wooden boatas a covering.

pamphlet_excerpts: Yourhands Gunwales Weight: Step in with yourhands on the gunwales, keep your weight low and centered, then quickly turn and sit on the midship seat.
Remember Sight Person: Remember to keep sight of the person who needs help andto push the bow of the boat in the direction you want to go.
Forward Momentum Advantage: Use this forward momentum to your advantage while you getin position and prepare to row.
Soon Seated Slipon: As soon as you are seated, slipon the life jacket and put the oars in the out position.
step_by_step_procedure: Lookover Shoulder Fix: Lookover your shoulder to fix your direction toward the person inthe water and begin rowing.
Approach Swimmer Thewind: Always make your approach to a swimmer into thewind or against the current.
Remember Wavesor Rough: Remember also that wavesor rough water can make launching from shoredangerous.
Comparatively Mild Interval: Usually, a comparatively mild interval willfollow a series of heavy waves.
